# How did I get into this mess?

## Sortition and representation

- Random selection of individuals to form a deliberative panel
- Used since ancient times, recently gaining renewed interest
- Descriptively representative in theory, enabling greater diversity and inclusion
- Selection is typically handled by a fairness-optimising algorithm (today: **LexiMin**), subject to quotas on each trait category

![Credit: Oivind Hovland/Ikon/Getty](Sortition_Graphic.png)

## The algorithm (LexiMin) {.small-text}

![@Flanigan2021FairAF](LexiMin.png)

Step (1): construct a maximally fair output distribution $\mathcal{D}$ over an optimal portfolio $\mathcal{P}$ of quota-compliant panels. Step (2): sample the distribution to select a final panel.

**The question this thesis asks:** satisfying quotas on each trait *separately* guarantees fairness of selection chances -- but does it guarantee a panel that actually *looks like* the population, once traits are considered *together*?

# So where in the process do we assess representativeness?

## Simulation design {.nostretch}

::: {style="font-size: 75%;"}

- Four-stage pipeline: **Population** (n = 100,000) &rarr; **Slice** (10% invited) &rarr; **Sample** (actual respondents) &rarr; **Panel** ($k$ = 50, via LexiMin)
- Two categorical traits: **age** (5 brackets) and **tenure** (Rent/Own/Other)
- Two populations: age & tenure **independent** or **associated** (negative age-renting relationship, via seeding + raking to preserve margins)
- Two response cases: **equal-chance** or **age-associated** (response probability rises with age) &rarr; four simulated respondent pools, each run through Panelot's LexiMin

:::

```{r}
#| label: population-slice-sample-panel-plot
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 2.4
#| out-width: 90%
box_w <- 1.55
box_h <- 0.85
xs <- c(0, 1.9, 3.8, 5.7)

pipeline_nodes <- data.frame(
  x = xs, y = 0,
  label = c("Population", "Slice\n(invited pool)", "Sample\n(respondent pool)", "Panel\n(k members)")
)
pipeline_edges <- data.frame(
  x = xs[1:3] + box_w / 2, xend = xs[2:4] - box_w / 2, y = 0,
  label = c("random 10% slice", "Bernoulli response\ntrials", "quota-constrained\nselection algorithm")
)

ggplot() +
  geom_rect(data = pipeline_nodes,
    aes(xmin = x - box_w / 2, xmax = x + box_w / 2, ymin = y - box_h / 2, ymax = y + box_h / 2),
    fill = "grey95", colour = "black") +
  geom_text(data = pipeline_nodes, aes(x = x, y = y, label = label),
    fontface = "bold", size = 3.6, lineheight = 0.9) +
  geom_segment(data = pipeline_edges, aes(x = x, xend = xend, y = y, yend = y),
    arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.18, "cm"), type = "closed"), linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_text(data = pipeline_edges, aes(x = (x + xend) / 2, y = y + 0.55, label = label),
    size = 2.9, lineheight = 0.9) +
  xlim(min(xs) - box_w / 2 - 0.1, max(xs) + box_w / 2 + 0.1) +
  ylim(-0.7, 1.0) +
  coord_fixed(ratio = 1.1) +
  theme_void()
```

## Does the panel preserve the association?

```{r}
#| label: fig-panel-vs-sample-example
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| out-width: 100%
invisible(capture.output(source("scripts/panel_visualiser.R")))
most_likely_panel_id <- which.max(cov_eq_source$lottery$return_probability)
plot_panel_vs_sample(cov_eq_source, most_likely_panel_id)
```

The sample (left) shows a smooth, gradual age-tenure relationship. The panel (right) satisfies the same marginal quotas, but its joint structure is far more blocky and uneven.

## Even with *no* true association...

```{r}
#| label: fig-panel-vs-sample-independent
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| out-width: 100%
ind_eq_source <- load_panel_source(file.path(lottery_dir, "lottery_ind_eq.csv"))
most_likely_ind_eq <- which.max(ind_eq_source$lottery$return_probability)
plot_panel_vs_sample(ind_eq_source, most_likely_ind_eq)
```

The independent population's sample is close to flat across age brackets (left) -- yet its panel (right) is, if anything, *more* distorted. There is no real association here for the panel to exaggerate: the distortion is a property of the quota mechanism itself.

## The headline result {.small-text}

```{r}
#| label: tbl-panel-association-summary
#| include: false
invisible(capture.output(source("scripts/performance_evaluator.R")))
file_order <- c("lottery_ind_eq.csv", "lottery_ind_ass.csv", "lottery_cov_eq.csv", "lottery_cov_ass.csv")
display_tbl <- lottery_summary[order(match(lottery_summary$file, file_order)), ]
```

::: {style="font-size: 75%;"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
knitr::kable(
  display_tbl[, c("file", "n_panels", "sample_cramers_v", "prop_sig_different")],
  col.names = c("Lottery file", "Panels", "Sample V", "Prop. sig. diff."),
  digits = c(0, 0, 3, 3),
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

:::

- Across **all four** simulated conditions (independent/associated population, equal-chance/age-skewed response), **`r round(min(lottery_summary$prop_sig_different) * 100, 1)`-100%** of feasible panels show an age-tenure association significantly different from their own sample
- True even for the **independent** population, where there is no association to distort in the first place
- Against a simple-random-sampling benchmark (500 draws of equal size), panels are flagged at a rate **roughly an order of magnitude higher** than chance

## Why does this happen? {.nostretch}

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="45%"}
- Quotas set **marginally** -- age and tenure counted separately, never jointly
- Meeting every quota says nothing about how categories *combine*
- A panel can hit every quota and still be badly skewed on intersections
- Invisible to standard pie/bar chart reporting
:::

::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r}
#| label: quota-vs-joint-schematic
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 4.3
#| out-width: 100%
make_quota_panel <- function(counts_mat, title) {
  rows <- c("A", "B", "C")
  cols <- c("Rent", "Own")
  row_totals <- rowSums(counts_mat)
  col_totals <- colSums(counts_mat)

  df <- expand.grid(row = rows, col = cols)
  df$count <- as.vector(counts_mat)

  row_labs <- paste0(rows, "\n(n=", row_totals, ")")
  col_labs <- paste0(cols, "\n(n=", col_totals, ")")
  names(row_labs) <- rows
  names(col_labs) <- cols

  ggplot(df, aes(x = col, y = row, fill = count)) +
    geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 1.2) +
    geom_text(aes(label = count), size = 6, fontface = "bold") +
    scale_fill_gradient(low = "grey95", high = "grey40", limits = c(0, 4), guide = "none") +
    scale_x_discrete(labels = col_labs, position = "top") +
    scale_y_discrete(labels = row_labs, limits = rev(rows)) +
    labs(title = title, x = NULL, y = NULL) +
    coord_fixed() +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
    theme(
      panel.grid = element_blank(),
      axis.text = element_text(colour = "black", face = "bold", size = 10),
      plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12, hjust = 0.5)
    )
}

# Same row/column quotas (4,4,4 / 6,6) -- different joint structure
skewed_mat <- matrix(c(4, 0,
                        1, 3,
                        1, 3), nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE)
balanced_mat <- matrix(c(2, 2,
                          2, 2,
                          2, 2), nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE)

p_skewed <- make_quota_panel(skewed_mat, "Skewed")
p_balanced <- make_quota_panel(balanced_mat, "Balanced")

p_skewed + p_balanced +
  plot_annotation(
    title = "Both satisfy identical quotas",
    theme = theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12, hjust = 0.5))
  )
```
:::

::::

::: {.notes}
LexiMin's quotas are set marginally -- a count per age bracket, a count per tenure category -- never jointly. Satisfying every marginal quota says nothing about how those categories combine within a selected panel. A panel can hit every quota count exactly and still be badly skewed on the intersections that matter for lived experience. This is invisible to the pie charts / bar charts typically used to report panel composition.
:::

[Watch the demo video](https://drive.google.com/file/d/14_uLDk7YKTWf6XqL-TCqphr7yGYmxCaX/view?usp=sharing){style="font-size: 150%;"}

## A framework for practitioners

::: {style="font-size: 105%; line-height: 2;"}
1. **Quota-based selection** -- still the right tool for fair marginal chances
2. **Intersectional check** -- before convening, not after
3. **Deliberate joint constraints** where a specific intersection matters
:::

::: {style="font-size: 105%;"}
Marginal quota satisfaction: **necessary, but not sufficient**.
:::

::: {.notes}
Quota-based selection (LexiMin, or future methods) remains the right tool for fair, robust marginal selection probabilities. An intersectional check -- like Intersection Inspector -- should sit between panel generation and convening, before members are contacted. Where a specific intersection matters for an engagement, deliberate joint-quota constraints or targeted recruitment are more defensible than trusting marginal quotas to deliver it incidentally. Marginal quota satisfaction should be treated as necessary, but not sufficient, evidence of a representative panel.
:::

## Limitations

::: {style="font-size: 95%; line-height: 2;"}

- Only **two** categorical variables simulated -- real panels typically use three or more
- Response rates elevated (30-50%) -- a **conservative, best-case** estimate
- Association strengths fixed for visibility, not drawn from real data
- Tool compares **two variables** at a time; levels sorted alphabetically

:::

::: {.notes}
Simulation uses only two categorical variables; real panels typically use three or more -- the gap is expected to compound, not shrink, as dimensionality grows. Response rates (30-50%) were deliberately elevated above typical civic-lottery rates (often < 10%), to keep cells populated enough to isolate the algorithm's behaviour -- results are a conservative, best-case estimate. Association strengths were fixed at values chosen for visibility, not drawn from a specific real-world dataset. Intersection Inspector shows two variables' joint structure at a time, and sorts uploaded levels alphabetically (a problem for ordinal variables specifically).
:::

## Future research

::: {style="font-size: 100%; line-height: 2.4;"}
- Extend to **more than two** variables
- Revisit with the **Goldilocks** algorithm once released
- Selection methods with **joint** constraints, not after-the-fact checks
:::

::: {.notes}
Extend simulation beyond two variables to test how severely distortion scales with added demographic categories. Revisit with the Goldilocks algorithm once released -- does its handling of selection-probability floors/ceilings affect intersectional preservation? More directly: selection methods that build in joint, intersectional constraints alongside marginal quotas, rather than checking for intersectionality after the fact.
:::
